title: 2026 and the 4-year global temperature average on track to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels | Copernicus
text:
2026 and the 4-year global temperature average on track to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels | Copernicus

# 2026 and the 4-year global temperature average on track to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels 

 Date: 11th November 2026 

- Record high sea surface temperatures persist
- River flows remain exceptionally low
- Second lowest Antarctic sea ice extent for October
- Footnotes

This year is now virtually certain 1 to surpass 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, becoming the second year on record to do so, following 2024. The average global temperature for 2023 to 2026 is also expected to exceed 1.5°C beyond the pre-industrial baseline, as reported in the latest Climate Bulletin by the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S).

Annual global surface air temperature anomalies (°C) from 1967 to 2026 relative to the 1850–1900 pre-industrial reference period. The range shown in red represents the 95% prediction interval for 2026, calculated using a statistical model fitted to past ERA5 data. Data source: ERA5. Credit: C3S/ECMWF.

> “October has continued the pattern of remarkable global warmth, with record global and surface ocean temperatures. An exceptionally strong El Niño is adding further heat to a climate already warmed by human activities, while 2026 is on track to become the second calendar year above 1.5°C. Particularly significant is that the four-year average is also expected to exceed 1.5°C, highlighting how sustained this period of global warmth has become.” Samantha Burgess, Head of Strategic Climate Research at ECMWF

According to a statistical prediction based on ERA5 data up to October this year, 2026 is most likely to be the second-warmest year ever recorded. It also has about a one in five chance of tying or exceeding 2024 – currently the warmest year on record.

With a global average surface air temperature of 15.35°C, 1.75°C above the estimated 1850-1900 pre-industrial baseline, October 2026 was the warmest October ever recorded. It was also the third consecutive month to exceed 1.5°C above the pre-industrial reference.

Meanwhile, Europe saw its second warmest October on record, behind only 2022. In contrast to the record-breaking temperatures seen across western Europe in recent months, temperatures were closer to average there in October and most above average across Fennoscandia and far-eastern Europe. 

## Record high sea surface temperatures persist 

October saw the highest average sea surface temperature (SST) outside the polar regions – between 60°S and 60°N – ever recorded for the month, at 20.95°C, marking the fifth consecutive month to see record monthly temperatures.

Sea surface temperature anomaly for October 2026 relative to the October average for the 1991-2020 reference period. Data source: ERA5. Credit: C3S/ECMWF.

Across much of the tropical Pacific, SSTs remained exceptionally high in October as El Niño conditions continued to intensify. The monthly average SST in the Niño 3.4 region – the area used to monitor El Niño conditions – reached a record high of 29.94°C, exceeding the peaks of previous very strong El Niño events.

Around Europe, record high SSTs for October were seen along the Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean. It also marked the fourth consecutive month to see record monthly SSTs across these areas. 

## River flows remain exceptionally low 

Much of central and eastern Europe saw exceptionally low river flows persist in October, affecting the Rhine, Danube and Vistula. By contrast, dry conditions eased in parts of western Europe during October, compared with September, including regions of Iberia, France and Italy.

Anomalies and extremes in monthly average river flow in October 2026. The extreme categories ('highest’ and ‘lowest’) are based on rankings for 1992–2026 for the month of October. The other categories describe how river flow compares to the distribution during the 1992–2020 reference period for the month of October. ‘Much higher/lower than average’ – higher/lower than 90% of river flow values; ‘higher/lower than average’ – than 66% of river flow values; ‘near average’ – within the middle 33%. Only rivers with drainage areas greater than 1000 km 2 are shown. Data: EFAS. Credit: CEMS/C3S/ECMWF.

Eastern Iberia, Iceland, the UK and Ireland, much of France and Germany, southern Scandinavia, the northwestern Black Sea region, Greece and Türkiye experienced wetter than average conditions in October. Heavy rainfall and flooding affected several countries among these regions, including the UK and Ireland, Spain, Greece and Türkiye.

Beyond Europe, wetter than average conditions were seen in Alaska, part of the southern USA and northern Mexico, a large region of central Asia, parts of China and Korea, Chile, southern Argentina and southeastern Brazil, southernmost Africa, Madagascar, and western and central Australia. In several of these areas, heavy precipitation, in some cases related to tropical cyclones, led to flooding.

## Second lowest Antarctic sea ice extent for October 

The sea ice extent around Antarctica for October was 1.7 million km 2 (9.3%) below average, making it the second lowest ever recorded for the month, behind only 2023. Sea ice cover was exceptionally low in the Amundsen–Bellingshausen Sea sector, which was associated with unusually warm conditions over the region and persistent northerly winds.

Time series of monthly mean Antarctic sea ice extent anomalies for all October months from 1979 to 2026. The anomalies are expressed as a percentage of the October average for the period 1991-2020. Data source: EUMETSAT OSI SAF Sea Ice Index v3.0. Credit: C3S/ECMWF/EUMETSAT. 

Meanwhile, the Arctic sea ice extent for October was 700,000 km 2 (8.5%) below average – the 13th lowest on record for the month.

## Footnotes 

 1 “Virtually certain” means a probability of more than 99%, according to the statistical model.
